title: Rise and Consolidation of Nazi Power, 1933–1934
description: Why Germans turned to the Nazis, Hitler as Chancellor, the Reichstag Fire.
content_html:
Why Did Germans Turn to the Nazis?

By 1932 the Nazi Party had become the largest party in Germany. Several overlapping factors explain this surge. The Great Depression, which began in 1929, had caused approximately six million Germans to lose their jobs by early 1932. Weimar's coalition governments seemed paralysed and ineffective. Traditional parties of the centre and left lost the confidence of voters who blamed them for Germany's humiliation under the Treaty of Versailles and the economic disaster.

The Nazis offered simple, powerful messages: a strong Germany restored to greatness, punishment of the groups they blamed for Germany's troubles (Jews, communists, the Weimar politicians), full employment, and national unity. Their propaganda — mass rallies, striking imagery and the cult of Hitler's personal leadership — was carefully managed. The party also ran effective local organisations that provided welfare in the early Depression years, winning grassroots loyalty. While no single group exclusively supported the Nazis, they drew heavily from the middle class, rural voters, Protestants and the young.

Key Fact

In the July 1932 election the Nazis won 37.4% of votes — their highest ever in a free election. In November 1932 support fell to 33.1%, suggesting their peak support had passed. Hitler was nonetheless appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933.

Hitler as Chancellor, January 1933

President Hindenburg disliked and distrusted Hitler but was persuaded by advisers — notably Franz von Papen — that Hitler could be appointed chancellor and then controlled. Papen believed conservative politicians in the cabinet would act as a check on Hitler. On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Hitler as chancellor. This proved a catastrophic miscalculation. Within eighteen months Hitler had used a series of legal and semi-legal steps to transform Germany from a democratic republic into a one-party dictatorship.

The Reichstag Fire and the Emergency Decree

On 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building was set on fire. A young Dutch communist named Marinus van der Lubbe was found at the scene and arrested. Hitler immediately claimed the fire was evidence of a communist plot to overthrow the government. The next day Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending civil liberties including freedom of speech, press and assembly, and allowing arrest without trial. Over 4,000 communists were arrested in the following weeks, removing the Nazi Party's main political rivals from the election campaign then under way.

On 23 March 1933, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which gave Hitler the power to make laws without consulting parliament for four years. To pass it required a two-thirds majority. The Nazis had arrested communist deputies and intimidated opposition members. Only the Social Democrats voted against. SA and SS troops lined the chamber. The Enabling Act was the legal foundation of Hitler's dictatorship; from this point, Germany's government operated outside the Weimar Constitution.

Gleichschaltung: Coordinating German Society

Gleichschaltung — literally 'co-ordination' or 'bringing into line' — was the process by which the Nazis extended their control over every institution in Germany during 1933. Trade unions were banned in May 1933 and replaced by the Nazi Labour Front. All political parties other than the NSDAP were banned by July 1933. State governments were stripped of their independence and replaced by Nazi-appointed governors. Newspapers, radio and film came under the control of Joseph Goebbels's new Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.

The Night of the Long Knives, June 1934

The SA (Sturmabteilung — the Nazi stormtroopers) numbered approximately three million by 1934 and its leader, Ernst Röhm, demanded that the SA absorb the army into a 'people's militia'. This alarmed the regular army, which Hitler needed to rearm Germany and secure his regime. Conservative politicians and business leaders also feared the SA's radical, street-fighting culture. Over the weekend of 29–30 June 1934, Hitler ordered the SS and Gestapo to arrest and execute SA leaders. Röhm was shot in his prison cell.

The purge — known as the Night of the Long Knives — killed approximately 85 to 200 people, including Röhm and other SA leaders, along with conservative opponents like former chancellor Kurt von Schleicher. The purge demonstrated the ruthlessness of the Nazi regime and reassured the army that its position was secure under Hitler.

Key Fact

After President Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of chancellor and president, declaring himself Führer and commander-in-chief. The army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler. Germany was now a full dictatorship.

The Police State

Control was maintained through a network of terror. The SS and Gestapo monitored, arrested and intimidated opponents. The Gestapo relied heavily on denunciations from ordinary citizens — neighbours, colleagues and family members reporting suspected disloyalty. Concentration camps had been established as early as March 1933 at Dachau; by 1934 they held political prisoners — communists, socialists, trade unionists and others deemed enemies of the state. Fear was an effective tool: people self-censored because they did not know who might report them.

By August 1934 Hitler held complete formal power: chancellor, president, supreme commander of the armed forces, and Führer of the Nazi Party. All other parties were banned, the press was controlled, civil liberties suspended. However, in practice the regime still relied on the cooperation of existing institutions — the civil service, the judiciary and the army — many of whose members were not committed Nazis. The consolidation of power was therefore more a dismantling of democratic safeguards than an overnight transformation of every aspect of German life.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark significance questions on the Enabling Act or the Night of the Long Knives, remember to address significance at the time AND over time. The Enabling Act matters at the time because it gave Hitler legal power to bypass parliament; over time because it was the legal foundation for all subsequent Nazi legislation. For 16-mark period essays on how Hitler consolidated power, structure your argument around key turning points (January 1933, March 1933, June 1934, August 1934) and weigh how far each step was planned versus opportunistic.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933 — not elected. President Hindenburg was persuaded that Hitler could be controlled. Within months the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933) and the Enabling Act (March 1933) had dismantled parliamentary democracy.
  • Gleichschaltung coordinated German society under Nazi control during 1933: trade unions banned, parties dissolved, state governments absorbed, press controlled.
  • The Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) eliminated the SA leadership and secured the army's loyalty. Hindenburg's death in August 1934 allowed Hitler to merge chancellor and president into the role of Führer, completing the dictatorship.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act (1933).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Enabling Act gave Hitler the power to make laws without consulting the Reichstag for four years. This meant he could govern by decree and bypass all parliamentary checks, effectively ending democratic government in Germany. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification with no development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hitler's consolidation of power between January 1933 and August 1934.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The Reichstag Fire Decree (28 February 1933) suspended civil liberties and allowed the Nazis to arrest communist opponents before the March 1933 elections. [2 marks]
• The Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) saw Hitler order the murder of SA leader Ernst Röhm and others, reassuring the army and eliminating a potential rival power base. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement of a reason.
Developing: Reason identified with some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Deep analysis of the mechanism, relating the cause to the broader context of Depression and democratic failure.
Example content: The Great Depression caused mass unemployment — approximately six million unemployed by early 1932. Weimar's coalition governments appeared unable to tackle the crisis, rotating chancellors through emergency decrees. This collapse of faith in mainstream parties drove voters towards the Nazis, making them the largest Reichstag party in July 1932 with 37.4% of votes. This electoral strength, combined with Papen's persuasion of Hindenburg that Hitler could be 'tamed', led to the appointment.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Enabling Act (1933) for Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores the longer-term consequences and links to later developments.
Example content: The Enabling Act gave Hitler the legal authority to govern without the Reichstag for four years. As a direct consequence, the Nazis used this power to ban all other political parties by July 1933 and to pass laws attacking Jews, trade unions and political opponents — all without parliamentary scrutiny. The Act also set the precedent that Hitler's will, not constitutional law, was the supreme source of authority in Germany.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) for Hitler's consolidation of power.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what happened.
Developing: Some assessment of importance.
Secure: Explains significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs significance against other consolidation steps; argues the Night of the Long Knives was decisive or contextualises it within the overall process.
At the time: Eliminated the SA leadership as a rival power base; secured the loyalty of the German army, which Hitler needed for rearmament.
Over time: Demonstrated the regime's willingness to use extrajudicial murder; the SS and Gestapo became the dominant instruments of control, foreshadowing the terror state.

practice_questions.text:
'Hitler's appointment as chancellor in January 1933 was the most important step in his consolidation of power.' How far do you agree?
In your answer, consider the importance of January 1933 alongside other key steps, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, limited or no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides, limited evidence, weak conclusion.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs each step (January 1933, Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung, Night of the Long Knives, August 1934 merger of roles) against each other and reaches a nuanced conclusion.

Arguments for: Without becoming chancellor Hitler had no access to state power; all other steps depended on being in that position.
Arguments against: Appointment alone was limited — the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave genuine legislative power; the Night of the Long Knives secured army loyalty; the August 1934 merger of president and chancellor gave Hitler supreme authority.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of the vote did the Nazis win in July 1932?
flashcard_questions.a: 37.4%, their highest ever share in a free election.

flashcard_questions.q: Who persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor?
flashcard_questions.a: Franz von Papen, who believed Hitler could be controlled.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933) do?
flashcard_questions.a: Suspended civil liberties and allowed arrest without trial.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Enabling Act passed, and what did it do?
flashcard_questions.a: March 1933; gave Hitler power to make laws without the Reichstag for four years.
Nazi policy coordinating all institutions under party control in 1933.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Night of the Long Knives?
Why did Hitler order the killing of Ernst Röhm?
flashcard_questions.a: Röhm wanted the SA to absorb the army, threatening Hitler's alliance with the military.

flashcard_questions.q: What oath did the German army swear after Hindenburg's death in August 1934?
flashcard_questions.a: A personal oath of loyalty to Hitler as Führer.
Germany's secret state police, responsible for arresting and interrogating political opponents.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the first concentration camp established at Dachau?
Why did only the Social Democrats vote against the Enabling Act?
flashcard_questions.a: Communist deputies had been arrested; other parties were intimidated by SA troops surrounding the chamber.

glossary_terms.definition: The National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), led by Adolf Hitler, which ruled Germany as a dictatorship from 1933.
An emergency decree signed on 28 February 1933 suspending civil liberties and enabling mass arrests of political opponents.
A law passed in March 1933 giving Hitler the power to make laws without consulting the Reichstag, forming the legal basis of his dictatorship.
The Nazi policy of coordination, bringing all German institutions — parties, unions, press, state governments — under party control in 1933.
The purge on 29–30 June 1934 in which Hitler ordered the SS and Gestapo to murder the SA leadership, including Ernst Röhm.
The SS (Schutzstaffel) was Hitler's elite guard; the Gestapo was the secret state police. Together they formed the backbone of Nazi terror and surveillance.
Hitler's title meaning 'leader', assumed in August 1934 when he merged the offices of chancellor and president after Hindenburg's death.
